items.title: One current truth, kept by code
items.summary: What is current and what is retired lives in ONE registry. A retired concept is data: a pattern, the context in which naming it is still true, and the truth that replaced it. The same scan runs on every push, in the test suite, in the rehearsal and on every episode.

evidence.source: Gloaguen et al., Evaluating AGENTS.md, arXiv 2602.11988
evidence.finding: agents obey repository context files; such files do not generally raise success and raise cost by more than 20%, so a wrong or long file is a direct loss

evidence.source: Chroma, Context Rot (Hong, Troynikov, Huber)
evidence.finding: reliability falls as input grows; distractors close in topic to the answer hurt most

items.title: Reference docs are rendered from the code, never typed
items.summary: The system reference is generated from the live code (facts, checks, settings, jobs, tabs, modules). A test fails when the committed file differs, so a doc can not state a number the code does not hold.

evidence.source: Grafana Loki CI step: check generated documentation
evidence.finding: CI fails when generated reference docs differ from the committed file

evidence.source: Fern, Stopping schema drift
evidence.finding: derive docs from one definition; treat drift as a build failure

items.title: History is archived whole and marked, never deleted, never followed
items.summary: A replaced document moves to the archive folder under a first line that says it is historical and names what replaced it; the text under that line is left unedited. Current docs may name the archive only while saying it is history.

evidence.source: M. Fowler, Architecture Decision Record (bliki); Backstage ADR docs
evidence.finding: accepted records are never rewritten or deleted; they are superseded with a pointer to the replacement

items.title: Ratchet baseline for unavoidable mentions
items.summary: Code that must name an old value (a one-time setting move) is listed in a baseline by file and rule, with a count and a reason. One more hit fails; one fewer also fails until the entry is pruned. The list can only shrink.

evidence.source: ESLint, Introducing bulk suppressions
evidence.finding: baseline existing violations by count per file and rule; report new ones at once; prune stale suppressions

items.title: The build chat's rule file is short, and wording is not enforcement
items.summary: The rule file a build chat loads holds only the non-obvious rules of this codebase and stays under 200 lines. Every rule that matters also has a check, because a context file is context, not enforcement.

evidence.source: Anthropic, Claude Code memory docs
evidence.finding: target under 200 lines; specific and concise instructions are followed more reliably; CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration

evidence.source: Gloaguen et al., Evaluating AGENTS.md, arXiv 2602.11988
evidence.finding: repository overviews do not help; only non-standard practices are worth writing

items.title: B1 build takeaway: scan what the code says about itself
items.summary: Generating the system doc from the code and then scanning it found stale statements inside LIVE settings notes that no search of the docs folder could find. Scan what the code says about itself, not only the documents. Keep current docs one fact per line: the rules are line-based.

evidence.source: v12 build, batch B1
evidence.finding: first scan: 33 retired-concept hits + 11 dead paths across the rule file, ledger, build prompt, Mission Control guide and 5 settings notes; after B1: 0

items.title: Executing a decision means retiring what it replaces
items.summary: When a decision replaces a value, register the old value as a retired concept BEFORE searching by hand. The scan found a fourth viewer line with the old cadence that a manual search had missed, and the generated system doc is what exposed the ledger-versus-code mismatch in the first place.

evidence.source: v12 build, batch B1b
evidence.finding: manual search found 3 of 4 lines; the retired rule found the 4th on its first run

items.title: Knowledge leaves the Palace through one guarded doorway
items.summary: Every playbook is built by one function whose first step is the status-and-date guard. A retired, superseded, expired or merely proposed item can never reach a prompt, whatever label it carries: memory systems that only LABEL a revoked fact keep serving it.

evidence.source: Shen, Toyoda, Leung, Revoked but Still Authoritative, arXiv 2609.08258
evidence.finding: five soft-revocation memory systems, 9 scenarios x 9 models: no system enforces revocation by default; a visible revoked record is returned, outranks its replacement and leads the agent to act on it; a guard that withholds it fixes this

items.title: Withdrawn knowledge takes its descendants with it
items.summary: When an item is retired or superseded, everything derived from it is sent back for re-validation by code in the same call. Readers are never trusted to check where a piece of knowledge came from: models rarely do.

evidence.source: Nakayashiki, When Stale Constraints Go Unchecked, arXiv 2608.25553
evidence.finding: 16 models: a memory whose source had been withdrawn still drove the decision in 77.3 / 74.7 / 74.7% of episodes; provenance was inspected in about 1 episode in 5; a freshness cue did not help

items.title: Limits are served first and never vanish silently
items.summary: Limits - the owner's words, policy rules, failure lessons - come first in every playbook and hold a reserved share of it. A stale technique is dropped until re-validated; a stale limit keeps being served, marked review due, and is reported.

evidence.source: Nakayashiki, When Stale Constraints Go Unchecked, arXiv 2608.25553
evidence.finding: a one-sentence rule that prefers memories stating a limit recovered +89.3 points on decisions where the constraint limits the tempting action

items.title: Memory is itemised and merged by code, never rewritten by a model
items.summary: The organisation's memory is a set of small items changed by small merges in code. A model is never asked to rewrite the whole memory: that collapses it into a vague summary. Size is held by caps per kind that displace the lowest-value item.

evidence.source: Zhang et al., Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), arXiv 2510.04618, ICLR 2026
evidence.finding: itemised bullets + deterministic non-model delta merges: +10.6% on agent tasks, +8.6% finance, 86.9% lower adaptation latency; full rewrites cause context collapse; needs a reliable outcome signal

items.title: Nothing enters the Palace without dated evidence
items.summary: Every item needs at least one dated source, and its trust is computed by code from the kind of evidence. Text typed by viewers or found on the web is data: it never becomes an accepted item without assessment, and text that reads like an instruction to a model is refused.

evidence.source: Dash et al., From Untrusted Input to Trusted Memory (MPBench), arXiv 2606.04329
evidence.finding: one hostile memory write has long-term influence; 4 write channels, 9 structural weaknesses; agents that write and read memory more eagerly are more exploitable; prompt-injection defences do not cover it

items.title: A playbook is deterministic and named by its own text
items.summary: The same Palace state always gives a byte-identical playbook, and the playbook id is the hash of its text. The cached prompt prefix therefore survives until knowledge really changes, and the id is proof of exactly what a department was given.

evidence.source: Anthropic prompt-caching documentation
evidence.finding: a cache hit needs a 100% identical prefix; minimum cacheable length 512-4,096 tokens by model; cache reads cost 0.1x input or less

items.title: Keep everything, serve little
items.summary: Nothing is deleted - a replaced item is kept with a pointer to its successor - and each department gets only a small current slice under a hard cap, with the full record of any item fetched by id when it is needed.

evidence.source: Rasmussen et al., Zep: a temporal knowledge graph architecture for agent memory, arXiv 2501.13956
evidence.finding: contradicted facts are end-dated, not deleted; up to +18.5% accuracy and 90% lower latency on LongMemEval as context fell from about 115,000 to about 1,600 tokens

evidence.source: Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents
evidence.finding: find the smallest set of high-signal tokens; hybrid: preload a little, fetch the rest on demand

items.title: The life cycle of knowledge is data, and every move names who may make it
items.summary: An item is proposed, accepted, testing, proven or retired, superseded or expired. The legal moves are a table in code, each with the roles allowed to make it; the path is not a straight line, and an item earns 'proven' only from evidence of use measured by Growth & Learning.

evidence.source: Consortium for Service Innovation, KCS v6 Practices Guide, technique 5.2 (article states)
evidence.finding: Work in Progress / Not Validated / Validated / Archived; the life cycle is non-linear; an article is validated by successful reuse; archive instead of delete

items.title: Google Sheets limits shape the Palace index
items.summary: The Sheets API allows 300 requests a minute per project and 60 per user, advises payloads under 2 MB, and a cell holds 50,000 characters. So one index row carries everything a playbook needs (one read builds it), long bodies live outside the Sheet, and writes are batched.

evidence.source: Google Sheets API usage limits
evidence.finding: 300 read and 300 write requests a minute per project, 60 per user per project; 2 MB payload recommended; 180 s request timeout; HTTP 429 when exceeded

items.title: Small knowledge bases are ranked by tags and keywords in code
items.summary: For a few hundred short items, department, stage, tag and weighted keyword matching in code is enough: it costs nothing, is deterministic and adds no dependency. An embedding scorer is worth adding only if the Palace outgrows it or queries become paraphrase-heavy.

evidence.source: BM25 wins at scale (2026 scaling study, as reported; primary id not verified)
evidence.finding: keyword ranking beat dense retrieval and agent search on large corpora; at the smallest sizes exact matching with reasoning was enough
